editorial.headline: Second-Hand Personal Goods: Nationally Open, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing used watches, clocks and jewellery is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium prevents registration there today.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this retail activity in Bali today, even though it is open nationally to up to 100% foreign ownership. The activity is the retail sale of used personal accessories: notably pre-owned watches, clocks and jewellery. It is a focused retail classification, defined by the goods being second-hand personal items rather than by an expansive claim over the broader resale market.

Nationally, the position is direct. The activity is marked **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership of 100%. It is also open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. For a business whose proposed operation falls within this scope, the national record therefore permits a fully foreign-owned PMA structure; there is no lower national foreign-ownership ceiling stated for this activity.

Bali changes that conclusion decisively. The Bali status is **BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO**. At the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and the activity is consequently blocked by Bali’s moratorium of May 13, 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently. This is not a qualification to be managed around in the registration narrative: for PMA registration in Bali, the activity is blocked.

That split deserves to be read in the right order. The national framework says the activity is open and can carry 100% foreign ownership; Bali’s provincial PMA rule says it cannot be registered there today. Anyone considering this used-personal-goods retail activity should therefore distinguish the national ownership position from the Bali registration outcome, rather than treating national openness as permission to establish the PMA activity on the island.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness permits 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA rule blocks registration of this activity on the island.
